sources.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology, U.S. Department of Commerce

sources.locator: Section 1.3.3.14, Histogram: purpose, definition, and questions the histogram answers
sources.license: US Government work; NIST states that information on its sites is public information and may be distributed or copied, with credit requested

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that a histogram summarises the distribution of a univariate dataset and displays location, spread, skewness, outliers, and multiple modes; that it is built by splitting the range into equal-sized bins that the user may define arbitrarily or by rule; and that dividing bin counts by the number of observations gives bar heights that are the proportion of the data in each class. All wording, the cohort, the binning convention, and every example in this lesson are original. NIST copyright guidance at https://www.nist.gov/oism/copyrights states that NIST information is public information that may be distributed or copied and requests appropriate credit.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that a scatter plot checks for a relationship between two variables and is used to ask whether they are related, whether any relationship is linear or non-linear, whether the variation in one changes across values of the other, and whether outliers are present. The sixty paired values, the reading procedure, and the wording in this lesson are original. sources.title: Data visualisation: charts
sources.version: Policy store guidance, online version retrieved 2026-07-25; no publication or revision date is stated on the page
sources.locator: Sections on choosing a chart type, bar charts and the numerical axis, and line charts

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that published guidance matches a display type to the statistical relationship being shown (bars for magnitude and ranking, lines for time series, scatterplots for correlation, maps for spatial patterns), that readers perceive bars as proportional to one another so breaking the numerical axis of a bar chart distorts those relative proportions and is advised against with an alternative display suggested instead, and that breaking the vertical axis of a line chart is treated as acceptable where needed. No wording, table, figure, or example from the guidance is reproduced; the teaching examples and all prose are original. The site's terms of use at https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/terms-of-use/ place most content under the Open Government Licence v3.0 and separately withhold permission to reuse the site's images, so no image from the source is used or adapted.

sources.title: Data visualisation: tables
sources.version: Policy store guidance, online version retrieved 2026-07-25; no publication or revision date is stated on the page
sources.locator: Section on when a demonstration table is useful

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the facts that a table is recommended when readers need to compare values, read summary figures such as averages or totals, or handle quantities of very different sizes in one display, while charts are recommended for showing patterns, trends, and relationships. No wording, table layout, or example from the guidance is reproduced; the clinic and waiting-time tables in this lesson are original. Content is published under the Open Government Licence v3.0 per https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/terms-of-use/.

uses.rightsBasisEvidence: Used only for the reference values it states for the fasting plasma glucose test, namely 99 mg/dL or below as normal, 100 to 125 mg/dL as prediabetes and 126 mg/dL or above as diabetes, for the statement that a doctor will usually use a second test to confirm a diabetes diagnosis, and for the definition of fasting as nothing to eat or drink except sips of water. The cohort, the banded counts, and all wording in this lesson are original, and the lesson makes no diagnostic or treatment recommendation.
